text: Resampling changes the data to fix an imbalance. Class weights take the gentler route: leave the data alone, and change what a mistake costs. Tell the algorithm that missing a rare, valuable case is worse than raising a false alarm, and in scikit-learn that is often a single argument.

Most training algorithms minimize a loss that treats every row equally. When ninety-five percent of rows are not fraud, predicting not-fraud almost every time already gives a great accuracy. The five percent barely register. A weight of five on the rare class makes each of those rows count as five in the loss.

On five thousand rows, five percent positive, we train three logistic regressions. Plain, with no weights. Balanced, which sets each class weight from the sample and class counts, here about zero point five three and nine point five two. And a hand-picked one-to-five dictionary you choose yourself.

Judge it with a cost: a missed positive costs one hundred dollars, a false alarm costs five. Plain scores ninety-seven percent accuracy but only forty-four percent recall, for a total cost of thirty-seven hundred. Balanced drops accuracy to eighty-four percent but catches eighty-nine percent of positives, for a cost of just sixteen sixty.

Plain has the best accuracy and the worst cost. Balanced has the worst accuracy and the best cost, because a miss here is twenty times pricier than a false alarm. There's no universally right weight; the right one depends entirely on your costs.

Not every estimator takes class_weight. Scikit-learn's HistGradientBoostingClassifier doesn't, for one. Almost every fit method accepts sample_weight instead, and compute_sample_weight with the string balanced builds it from your labels. Inside a pipeline, pass it to the final step with a double-underscore keyword, like model__sample_weight.

A decision threshold changes only how you read probabilities, not what the model learned. Lowering the plain model's threshold to zero point zero five cut its cost from thirty-seven hundred to seventeen eighty-five. Try both, but tune on validation data, never on the test set.
